_note: DRIVER ENVELOPES — versioned DATA for docs/backlog/se-off-the-shelf-fabrication.md rung 3b (tool access). A screw you cannot reach is not fastened, and the geometry that decides it is the TOOL's, not the screw's: a hex key needs a swept circle for its long arm, a bit driver needs a straight cylinder, a ratchet needs both. Each tool is modelled as two solids above the head — a SHAFT (a cylinder of `shaft_radius_mm` standing `axial_mm` tall on the drive face) and an ARM (a disc of `swing_radius_mm`, `arm_thickness_mm` thick, at `swing_height_mm`), which is the whole swept volume of one turn. Millimetres throughout. CONFIDENCE, and it differs sharply by section: `hex_keys` is ISO 2936 (short arm l2 and the standard long arm), transcribed and exact. `bit_tools` is NOT a standard and never will be — it is the nominal geometry of ordinary bench tools (a 1/4-inch bit screwdriver, a stubby ratchet, a T-handle), rounded, and a shop whose tools differ should edit this file rather than argue with the finding. A tool that fits here fits in the model of it; whether it fits your hand is not modelled at all.

hex_keys.source: ISO 2936 (hexagon key sizes): `short_arm` is l2, `long_arm` is the standard-length arm.

bit_tools.title: bit in a stubby ratchet
bit_tools.note: The most forgiving in depth, the least in sweep — it wants a clear disc the size of a hand.

bit_tools.title: bit screwdriver
bit_tools.note: Needs a straight run to the head and almost no sweep — the tool for a screw down a hole.

bit_tools.title: T-handle driver
bit_tools.note: Sweeps high and narrow: the compromise when the head is recessed but there is room above.

drive_tools._note: Order is PREFERENCE, best first: what the shop reaches for when everything fits. Torx has no L-key entry because these ones are driven with bits.
